summary:
RAQEEB is an open web app that explains how NISAR radar sees change on Earth's surface, in plain language for non-experts. Radar works through cloud, ash and darkness, but its images are hard to read. RAQEEB turns them into short guided stories.

Users pick a force of change (volcano, earthquake, flood, glacier, farmland or sinking land) and open a place on the map. Each place walks through what happened, how radar sees it, and what changed. A before/after slider lets users compare dates, and our own change maps highlight where the signal got brighter or darker. We covered Kamchatka's volcanoes, the Alaska earthquake and glacier, the Venezuela earthquakes, and the Chókwè flood in Mozambique, where we estimated about 199 km² of new open water from calibrated HH data. Other documented NASA cases are included as text only, with no images we don't have.

Every number comes from our own analysis, and each place states its limits honestly. Users can also create a one-page report with images and a simple chart, then download or share it.

RAQEEB matters because after a disaster, roads and networks may be down. Radar shows where the land changed, so teams can decide where to look first.
details:
RAQEEB is a free, open web app that teaches people how NISAR radar sees change on Earth's surface.

How it works: The user opens a 3D globe, picks a force of change (volcano, earthquake, flood, glacier, farmland or sinking land) and selects a place. Each place is a short guided story: what happened, how radar sees it, what changed, and why it matters. A before/after slider compares two dates. Our own change maps show where the radar signal got brighter or darker. A "Create report" button builds a one-page summary with images and a simple chart that can be downloaded or shared as an image.

Benefits and impact: Radar works through cloud, ash and night, but its images are hard to read. RAQEEB makes them understandable for students, teachers and the public. It also shows how radar could help teams decide where to look first after a disaster, when roads and networks are down.

What we built: Four places use real NISAR images with our own analysis: Kamchatka volcanoes, the Alaska earthquake and glacier, the Venezuela earthquakes, and the Chókwè flood in Mozambique (about 199 km² of new open water from calibrated HH data). Other NASA cases (Mexico City, Antarctica, North Dakota, Maine, Nile Delta) are included as documented text cases. Every place states its limits, such as brightness-only comparison on 8-bit previews, so the app never claims more than the data shows.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page; globe.gl and Leaflet for the globe and maps; html2canvas for report export; Python (NumPy, image processing) for the change analysis; NISAR data and previews from NASA and the Alaska Satellite Facility.

Creativity: A guided "story" format with a cartoon radar character, honest limits on every case, and a one-click report make radar science easy to understand and share.
